intro: Count the eggs in a carton, the seats on a school bus, or the tiles on a kitchen floor. You could count them one at a time, but there is a faster way. Things that come in equal groups can be counted by multiplying. This unit starts there: what multiplying means, why 4 × 6 and 6 × 4 give the same answer, and how to break a hard fact into easy pieces.

Then the unit turns around. If 4 × 7 = 28, then 28 cookies shared by 4 friends gives 7 each. That is division, and it undoes multiplication. You will learn two ways to think about dividing, what to do when the groups do not come out even, and how to handle problems that take two steps. Along the way you will learn every fact through 10 × 10 with strategies, not just memory.

By the end you will be able to solve a word problem by picturing the groups, write the four facts in a fact family, divide with a remainder and decide what it means, and use an estimate to catch a wrong answer before it gets written down.
bigQuestion: How do multiplication and division work together to count, share and check the world around us?

timeline.t: Scribes in Babylon press multiplication tables into clay tablets
An Egyptian scroll shows multiplying by doubling and adding
Euclid's Elements explains dividing with remainders to find common measures
Mathematicians in India write numbers with place value and a zero
Al-Khwarizmi writes a book on calculating with those numerals
Fibonacci's Liber Abaci brings the new numerals and methods to Europe
William Oughtred uses the × sign for multiplication in a printed book
Blaise Pascal builds a machine with gears that adds and subtracts
The ÷ sign appears in a printed algebra book by Johann Rahn
Pocket calculators multiply and divide at the press of a key
You learn the facts and strategies that let you check any calculator

test.q: There are 7 boxes with 6 donuts in each box. How many donuts are there?

test.why: Three 9s are added, so it is 3 × 9 = 27.

test.q: An array has 5 rows of 7 chairs. How many chairs are there?

test.why: The commutative property: the order of the factors does not change the product, so 4 × 8 = 32.

test.q: A rectangle is 7 units by 7 units. What is its area?
test.why: Area is 7 × 7 = 49 square units. Adding 7 + 7 = 14 is not area.

test.q: Which number is a multiple of 8?
test.why: 8 × 6 = 48. The multiples of 8 are 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48; the others are not on the list.

test.q: 36 cookies are shared equally by 6 friends. How many does each friend get?
What number goes in the box? ? × 7 = 63
test.why: 7 × 9 = 63, so the missing factor is 9. Subtracting 63 − 7 = 56 is the mistake.

test.q: In 40 ÷ 8 = 5, which number is the dividend?
test.why: The dividend is the number being divided, 40. The divisor is 8 and the quotient is 5.
6 × 4 = 24, and 25 − 24 = 1. So 25 ÷ 4 = 6 R 1. A remainder of 5 is too big, since another 4 would fit.

test.q: Cars hold 5 people each. 23 people need rides. How many cars are needed?
test.why: 23 ÷ 5 = 4 R 3. Four cars hold 20, so the 3 extra people need a fifth car.

test.q: Ben buys 4 packs of 5 balloons, and 3 balloons pop. How many are left?

test.why: Multiply first: 2 × 3 = 6, then 10 − 6 = 4. Subtracting first gives 8 × 3 = 24, which breaks the rule.

write.prompt: Solve this problem and explain each step: A camp has 26 campers. Each tent holds 4 campers. How many tents does the camp need? Then explain how you know your answer is right, and what would change if the question asked how many campers are in the last tent.
tips: State your answer in a full sentence first.
Write the division sentence and show the remainder.
Say what the remainder means in this story and why you rounded up.
Check your work by multiplying back: quotient × divisor + remainder.
Answer the last question with a different number and say why it is different.

title: Multiplication and Division

chapters.title: What Multiplying Means
chapters.bigQuestion: How can one small fact, like 4 × 6 = 24, count muffins, seats, tiles and windows all at once?

story.title: The Day the Pattern Showed Up
story.kicker: Egg cartons, muffin tins and a bakery counter full of numbers that kept repeating.
paragraphs: Every Saturday, Rosa helps at her aunt's bakery on the North Side of Chicago. Her first job is eggs. The cartons come in a stack. Each carton holds 2 rows of 6 eggs. Rosa's aunt asks, "How many eggs in 5 cartons?" Rosa opens each one and starts counting: 1, 2, 3, 4… By the fourth carton she has lost her place twice.

Her cousin Dev laughs and points at one carton. "Look at it. Two rows. Six in each row. That's 12, every time. You don't need to count the eggs. Count the cartons." He taps the stack: 12, 24, 36, 48, 60. "Sixty eggs." Rosa checks one carton. Twelve. She checks another. Twelve. The pattern holds.

Next come the muffin tins. Each tin has 3 rows with 4 cups in a row. Rosa does not count cups this time. She counts one row, 4, and then counts by 4s: 4, 8, 12. Twelve muffins in a tin. Six tins in the oven means 12 six times: 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72. Seventy-two muffins. She writes it on the whiteboard before Dev can say it.

By noon Rosa is seeing the pattern everywhere. The window on the front of the shop has 4 rows of 5 panes. The cookie trays hold 6 rows of 8. The parking spots outside sit in 2 rows of 9. Same idea, every time: how many rows, how many in each row. Her aunt hands her a marker and says, "Write the rule."

Rosa writes: "Rows times how many in a row." Dev adds a sign she has seen before but never really used: ×. "That's the times sign," he says. "3 × 4 means three 4s. It's not a new kind of counting. It's counting groups, and the groups have to be equal." Rosa looks back at the egg cartons. Equal groups. That was the whole secret.
story.think: Where else in a bakery, a school or a bus could you find equal groups? Name one and say how many rows and how many in each row.

lessons.title: Counting Equal Groups
lessons.mainIdea: Multiplication counts equal groups: 4 groups of 6 is 4 × 6 = 24.
reading: Maya packs muffins for a bake sale. She has 4 boxes, and each box holds 6 muffins. Every box has the same number, so these are *equal groups*. To find the total, she could count the muffins one by one. That takes a long time. Instead she counts by 6s: 6, 12, 18, 24. Four boxes hold 24 muffins.

Math has a short way to write this. We say 4 groups of 6 and write 4 × 6 = 24. The sign × means *multiply*. The numbers you multiply, 4 and 6, are each called a *factor*. The answer, 24, is the *product*. The first factor tells how many groups. The second factor tells how many are in each group.

Groups only count as equal if every group has the same amount. Three bags with 5, 5 and 5 apples are equal groups: 3 × 5 = 15. Three bags with 5, 4 and 6 apples are not, even though the total is still 15. A common mistake is to multiply the number of groups by the total. Always multiply the groups by the amount in one group.

words.d: groups that all have the same number of things in them
to find the total of equal groups; the sign is ×
a number you multiply; in 4 × 6 = 24, both 4 and 6 are factors
the answer when you multiply; in 4 × 6 = 24, the product is 24

look.title: Count the Wheels
look.text: A parking lot has 7 cars. Each car has 4 wheels. Picture the cars in a row. Count by 4s as you walk past: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28. Seven cars have 28 wheels, so 7 × 4 = 28. Now picture 5 tricycles with 3 wheels each.
look.prompt: Write a multiplication sentence for the tricycles and find the product.

check.q: There are 5 boxes with 8 crayons in each box. How many crayons are there in all?
check.why: 5 × 8 = 40; count by 8s: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40. Adding 5 + 8 = 13 is a common mistake.

check.q: Which of these shows equal groups?
choices: 4 plates with 5 cookies on each plate
check.why: Equal groups all hold the same amount. Only the 4 plates with 5 each are equal: 4 × 5 = 20.

check.q: In 6 × 7 = 42, which number is the product?
check.why: The product is the answer to a multiplication. 6 and 7 are the factors; 6 × 7 = 42.

lessons.title: Adding the Same Number Again
lessons.mainIdea: Adding the same number over and over is multiplying: 5 + 5 + 5 is the same as 3 × 5.
reading: Jamal walks his neighbor's dog every day for a week. He earns $5 each time. To find his pay for 7 days, he could add: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 35. That is seven 5s added together. Adding the same number over and over is called *repeated addition*. Multiplication is a faster way to write it: 7 × 5 = 35.

You can turn any repeated addition into multiplication. Count how many times the number appears. That count is the first factor. The number being added is the second factor. So 9 + 9 + 9 + 9 = 4 × 9 = 36. And 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 × 2 = 12. Check: six 2s make 12. We also say 6 *times* 2.

Be careful: 6 × 2 means six 2s, not 6 + 2. A student who writes 6 × 2 = 8 has added the factors instead of multiplying. Another student might write 3 × 4 as 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 and get 12. That total is still correct, because three 4s and four 3s add to the same number. But the meaning of 3 × 4 is three groups of 4.

words.d: adding the same number again and again, like 5 + 5 + 5
another word for multiply; 3 times 4 means three 4s

look.title: Stacks of Quarters
look.text: A quarter is worth 25 cents. Nia has 4 quarters. She adds 25 + 25 + 25 + 25 and gets 100 cents, which is $1.00. She writes 4 × 25 = 100. Now think about 3 dimes. A dime is worth 10 cents.
look.prompt: Write the repeated addition and the multiplication for the 3 dimes. How many cents are they worth?

check.q: Which multiplication matches 8 + 8 + 8?
check.why: Three 8s are added, so it is 3 × 8. And 8 + 8 + 8 = 24, so 3 × 8 = 24.

check.q: What is 4 × 6 written as repeated addition?
check.why: 4 × 6 means four 6s: 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24. Writing 4 + 6 is adding the factors, which gives only 10.

check.q: Leo saves $6 a week for 5 weeks. How much does he save?
check.why: 5 × 6 = 30, or 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 30. Adding 5 + 6 = 11 is the mistake to avoid.

lessons.title: Rows and Columns
lessons.mainIdea: An array lines things up in rows and columns, and rows × how many in a row gives the total.
reading: An egg carton holds eggs in 2 rows with 6 in each row. Objects lined up in neat rows and columns make an *array*. A *row* goes across. A *column* goes up and down. To count the eggs, multiply the number of rows by how many are in each row: 2 × 6 = 12. A dozen eggs is 12.

A muffin tin might have 3 rows with 4 cups in each row. That array shows 3 × 4 = 12. Count the rows first, then count across one row. Do not count every cup; the array does that work for you. If you skip count by rows, you get 4, 8, 12. Same answer, and much faster than counting one by one.

Arrays are everywhere: windows on a building, seats in a theater, tiles on a floor. A classroom has 5 rows of desks with 6 desks in each row. That is 5 × 6 = 30 desks. A common mistake is adding rows and columns: 5 + 6 = 11. Eleven desks would not even fill two rows. Multiply, and 30 makes sense.

words.d: things arranged in equal rows and columns, like eggs in a carton
a line that goes across, from left to right
a line that goes up and down

look.title: Arrays Around You
look.cite: Totals counted from arrays you can find in a kitchen, a classroom and a game
look.prompt: Which two arrays have the same total? How can different rows give the same number?

check.q: A sticker sheet has 4 rows with 7 stickers in each row. How many stickers are there?
check.why: 4 rows × 7 = 28. Count by 7s: 7, 14, 21, 28. Adding 4 + 7 = 11 is the mistake.

check.q: An array has 6 rows of 3. Which multiplication shows it?
check.why: 6 rows with 3 in each row is 6 × 3 = 18.

check.q: A theater has 8 rows of 9 seats. Which is the best way to count the seats?
choices: Count every seat one at a time
check.why: Rows × seats in a row: 8 × 9 = 72. Counting one by one works but is slow, and 8 + 9 counts only 17.

lessons.title: Turn the Array Around
lessons.mainIdea: Turning an array shows that 3 × 5 and 5 × 3 have the same product; the order of the factors does not change it.
reading: Draw an array with 3 rows of 5 dots. It shows 3 × 5 = 15. Now turn your paper a quarter turn. The same dots now sit in 5 rows of 3. That is 5 × 3 = 15. Nothing was added or taken away, so the total must be the same. Turning the array is a picture of an important rule.

The rule is the *commutative property*: you can multiply two numbers in either *order* and get the same product. 4 × 7 = 28 and 7 × 4 = 28. 2 × 9 = 18 and 9 × 2 = 18. Commutative comes from the word commute, which means to move or switch places. The factors switch places, and the product stays the same.

This rule cuts your work in half. If you know 8 × 3 = 24, you also know 3 × 8 = 24. Learn 6 × 9 = 54, and 9 × 6 comes free. But be careful: subtraction does not work this way. 9 − 2 is 7, but 2 − 9 is not 7. Switching the numbers works for addition and multiplication only.

words.d: the rule that switching the order of the factors does not change the product: 3 × 5 = 5 × 3
which number comes first and which comes second

look.title: Two Ways to See 24
look.text: A baker sets out 4 trays with 6 rolls on each: 4 × 6 = 24. Her helper stacks the same rolls on 6 trays with 4 on each: 6 × 4 = 24. Same rolls, two arrays. Now picture 2 rows of 8 chairs, and then 8 rows of 2 chairs.
look.prompt: Draw both chair arrays. What are the two multiplication sentences, and what is the product?

check.q: If 7 × 6 = 42, what is 6 × 7?
check.why: The commutative property says the order does not matter: 6 × 7 = 7 × 6 = 42.

check.q: Which pair of facts shows the commutative property of multiplication?
check.why: 9 × 4 and 4 × 9 use the same factors in a different order and give the same product, 36.

check.q: You turn an array of 5 rows of 8 a quarter turn. What do you see?
choices: 8 rows of 5 with a different total
8 rows of 5 with the same total
check.why: Rows become columns: 8 rows of 5. Nothing was added, so the total is still 40.

lessons.title: Break a Factor Apart
lessons.mainIdea: To multiply a hard fact, break one factor into two easy parts, multiply each part, and add the two products.
reading: Suppose you forget 7 × 6. Draw an array with 7 rows of 6. Now draw a line after the fifth row. The top part is 5 rows of 6, which is 30. The bottom part is 2 rows of 6, which is 12. Add the parts: 30 + 12 = 42. So 7 × 6 = 42. You split one hard fact into two easy facts.

This is the *distributive property*. When you *break apart* one factor into two parts, you multiply each part and then add. 7 × 6 = (5 × 6) + (2 × 6) = 30 + 12 = 42. The other factor, 6, gets shared out to both parts. Try 8 × 4. Break 8 into 5 and 3: (5 × 4) + (3 × 4) = 20 + 12 = 32.

Choose parts you know well. Fives, twos and tens make good parts. For 9 × 7, break 9 into 5 and 4: (5 × 7) + (4 × 7) = 35 + 28 = 63. One mistake is forgetting to multiply the second part: 35 + 4 = 39 is wrong. Every part must be multiplied by the other factor before you add.

words.d: the rule that lets you break one factor into parts, multiply each part, and add: 7 × 6 = (5 × 6) + (2 × 6)
to split a number into two smaller numbers that add up to it, like 7 into 5 and 2

look.title: Splitting 6 × 8
look.text: Sam does not know 6 × 8. He draws 6 rows of 8 and cuts the array after row 3. Each part is 3 rows of 8, which is 24. He adds 24 + 24 = 48. So 6 × 8 = 48. Try the same idea on 6 × 7, splitting the 6 into 3 and 3.
look.prompt: What two smaller products do you get, and what is 6 × 7?

check.q: Which shows 8 × 6 broken apart correctly?
Kim splits 9 × 4 into (5 × 4) + (4 × 4). What are the two parts?

lessons.title: Rectangles and Area
lessons.mainIdea: A rectangle's area, counted in squares, is one side times the other, so a rectangle is a picture of a product.
reading: Cover a rectangle with same-size squares. The number of squares is its *area*. A rug is 3 squares wide and 8 squares long. Count the squares: 3 rows of 8 is 24 squares. You do not have to count every square. Multiply the two sides: 3 × 8 = 24. The rectangle is an array made of squares.

This rectangle is called an *area model*. It shows a product as a shape. A 6-by-7 rectangle has an area of 42 square units. A 10-by-10 rectangle has 100 square units. The two sides are the factors, and the area is the product. If each square is 1 foot on a side, the area is measured in square feet.

You can split an area model just like an array. A 6-by-7 rectangle can be cut into a 6-by-5 piece and a 6-by-2 piece. Their areas are 30 and 12, and 30 + 12 = 42. Later you will use this picture for bigger numbers, like 6 × 27. A common mistake is adding the sides: 6 + 7 = 13 counts edges, not squares.

words.d: the number of same-size squares that cover a flat shape
a rectangle drawn to show a multiplication; the sides are the factors and the area is the product
one square of the size you are counting with, like 1 square foot

look.title: Rectangles on Grid Paper
look.cite: Areas of rectangles drawn on 1-unit grid paper, found by counting squares
look.prompt: Which rectangle has the same area as a 3-by-8 rectangle? Draw both and check.

check.q: A garden is 4 feet by 9 feet. What is its area?
check.why: Area is side × side: 4 × 9 = 36 square feet. Adding 4 + 9 = 13 is not area.

check.q: A rectangle is 5 squares wide and 6 squares long. How many squares cover it?
check.why: 5 rows of 6 squares: 5 × 6 = 30.

check.q: A 7-by-6 rectangle is cut into two 7-by-3 pieces. What is the area of each piece?
check.why: Each piece is 7 × 3 = 21 square units. Together, 21 + 21 = 42, the whole rectangle.

lessons.title: Twos, Fours and Eights
lessons.mainIdea: Multiplying by 2 is doubling; double again for the 4s and once more for the 8s.
reading: Multiplying by 2 means *doubling*: 2 × 7 is 7 + 7 = 14. Doubles are easy for most people. Here is the useful part. Four is *double* two. So to multiply by 4, double, then double again. For 4 × 7: double 7 is 14, and double 14 is 28. So 4 × 7 = 28. Check by skip counting: 7, 14, 21, 28.

Eight is double four. To multiply by 8, double three times. For 8 × 6: double 6 is 12, double 12 is 24, double 24 is 48. So 8 × 6 = 48. Try 8 × 9: double 9 is 18, then 36, then 72. So 8 × 9 = 72. Doubling turns the hard eights into three easy steps.

Keep track of how many times you doubled. One double is × 2, two doubles is × 4, three doubles is × 8. A student who doubles 7 twice and calls it 8 × 7 = 28 has stopped too soon. 8 × 7 needs three doubles: 14, 28, 56. Write the steps down until they feel automatic.

words.d: adding a number to itself, which is the same as multiplying by 2
two times a number; the double of 6 is 12

look.title: A Doubling Chain for 9
look.text: Start with 9. Double once: 18, and that is 2 × 9. Double again: 36, and that is 4 × 9. Double once more: 72, and that is 8 × 9. Now start a chain with 7 and do the same three doubles.
look.prompt: What are 2 × 7, 4 × 7 and 8 × 7? Which step is hardest, and why?

check.q: Use doubling to find 4 × 8.
check.why: Double 8 is 16, double 16 is 32. So 4 × 8 = 32. Stopping at 16 is only 2 × 8.

check.q: What is 8 × 5?
check.why: Double 5 three times: 10, 20, 40. So 8 × 5 = 40.

check.q: Doubling 6 three times gives 12, 24, 48. Which fact does 48 show?
check.why: Three doubles is multiplying by 8, so 48 = 8 × 6.

lessons.title: Fives and Tens
lessons.mainIdea: Products of 10 end in 0, products of 5 end in 5 or 0, and a fives fact is half of the matching tens fact.
reading: Count by tens: 10, 20, 30, 40. Every product of 10 ends in a zero, and the other factor sits in front. A *tens fact* like 10 × 7 = 70 or 10 × 3 = 30 is quick to see. Look at a dime, worth 10 cents. Six dimes are 6 × 10 = 60 cents. Tens facts are the fastest facts on the table.

Five is *half* of ten. So a *fives fact* is half of a tens fact. 5 × 8 is half of 10 × 8. Half of 80 is 40, so 5 × 8 = 40. For 5 × 7, half of 70 is 35. Notice the pattern: products of 5 end in 5 or 0. Odd numbers times 5 end in 5, like 5 × 3 = 15. Even numbers times 5 end in 0, like 5 × 4 = 20.

Nickels show fives in action. A nickel is 5 cents. Nine nickels are 9 × 5 = 45 cents. A clock shows fives too. Each number on a clock face marks 5 minutes. The minute hand at the 4 means 4 × 5 = 20 minutes past. A student who writes 5 × 6 = 35 has counted one five too many; 5 × 6 = 30, and 30 ends in 0 because 6 is even.

words.d: a multiplication with 10 as a factor, like 10 × 7 = 70
a multiplication with 5 as a factor, like 5 × 7 = 35
one of two equal parts; half of 80 is 40

look.title: Nickels and Dimes
look.cite: U.S. coin values: a nickel is 5 cents, a dime is 10 cents
look.prompt: Why is a pile of nickels always worth half of the same number of dimes?

check.q: What is 10 × 9?
check.why: A tens fact puts the other factor in front of a 0: 10 × 9 = 90.

check.q: The minute hand points to the 7. How many minutes past the hour is it?
check.why: Each clock number marks 5 minutes, so the 7 means 7 × 5 = 35 minutes.

check.q: Which product of 5 is correct?
check.why: 5 × 8 is half of 10 × 8 = 80, so 40. The others are off by one five: 5 × 4 = 20, 5 × 7 = 35, 5 × 9 = 45.

lessons.title: The Nines Pattern
lessons.mainIdea: For a nines fact, the tens digit is one less than the other factor and the two digits add to 9; or take 10 × the number and subtract the number.
reading: Nines look hard, but they hide a pattern. Write the nines facts: 9, 18, 27, 36, 45, 54, 63, 72, 81, 90. Look at each *digit*. In 18, 1 + 8 = 9. In 27, 2 + 7 = 9. In 63, 6 + 3 = 9. The digits of every nines product up to 9 × 10 add to 9. That gives you a way to check your answer.

Here is the *nines pattern* as a shortcut. For 9 × 7, the tens digit is one less than 7, so it is 6. The ones digit must make the digits add to 9, so it is 3. The answer is 63. For 9 × 4: tens digit 3, ones digit 6, so 36. Check by adding: 3 + 6 = 9. It works for 9 × 1 through 9 × 10.

Another way uses tens. Nine is one less than ten, so 9 × 7 is 10 × 7 minus one 7. That is 70 − 7 = 63. And 9 × 8 is 80 − 8 = 72. Both routes give the same answer, which is a good check. A student who writes 9 × 6 = 56 should notice that 5 + 6 = 11, not 9. The real answer is 54.

words.d: in 9 × 1 through 9 × 10, the two digits of the product add to 9
one of the symbols 0 to 9 that make up a number; 63 has the digits 6 and 3

look.title: Two Routes to 9 × 8
look.text: Route 1: the tens digit is 8 − 1 = 7, and the ones digit is 9 − 7 = 2, so 72. Route 2: 10 × 8 = 80, then 80 − 8 = 72. Both routes agree. Now try both routes on 9 × 5.
look.prompt: What do you get each way? Do the digits of your answer add to 9?

check.q: What is 9 × 6?
check.why: Tens digit 5, ones digit 4: 54. Check: 60 − 6 = 54, and 5 + 4 = 9.

check.q: Which nines fact must be wrong, because its digits do not add to 9?
check.why: 6 + 2 = 8, not 9. The real answer is 9 × 7 = 63. The other three have digits that add to 9.

check.q: Use tens to find 9 × 4.
check.why: 10 × 4 = 40, and one less four is 40 − 4 = 36.

lessons.title: Multiples and the Table
lessons.mainIdea: A multiple of a number is that number times a whole number, and the multiplication table is full of patterns.
reading: The *multiples* of 3 are what you get when you multiply 3 by 1, 2, 3 and so on: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18. Skip counting lists the multiples. Every multiple of 2 is even. Every multiple of 5 ends in 5 or 0. Every multiple of 10 ends in 0. Is 24 a multiple of 4? Yes, because 4 × 6 = 24.

A *multiplication table* lists products in a grid. The row for 4 reads 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 and so on. Find 6 × 7 by going to the row for 6 and the column for 7. They meet at 42. Because of the commutative property, the table is a mirror across its diagonal. The row for 6 matches the column for 6.

The diagonal holds the *square numbers*: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100. Each comes from a number times itself, like 7 × 7 = 49. Each is the area of a square. Look for more patterns. In the row for 6, every product is even. Going down any column, each number grows by the same amount.

words.d: a number times a whole number; 12 is a multiple of 3 because 3 × 4 = 12
a grid that lists the products of the numbers 1 to 10 (or more)
a number times itself, like 5 × 5 = 25

look.title: The Row for 7
look.cite: One row of the multiplication table
look.prompt: How much does each product grow by? Do the products switch between odd and even? Why?

check.q: Which number is a multiple of 6?
check.why: 6 × 7 = 42. The multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42; 26, 32 and 40 are not on the list.

check.q: Which is a square number?
check.why: 36 = 6 × 6, a number times itself. The others are not.

check.q: On the table, the row for 8 and the column for 4 meet at what number?
check.why: 8 × 4 = 32. Adding gives 12, and 28 and 24 are 7 × 4 and 6 × 4.

lessons.title: Solving Word Problems
lessons.mainIdea: Find the groups and the size of each group, write the multiplication, solve it, then check that the answer fits the story.
reading: A *word problem* tells a story with numbers hidden in it. Read: "A Chicago bus has 6 rows of seats on one side, with 2 seats in each row. How many seats are on that side?" Ask two questions. How many groups? 6 rows. How many in each group? 2 seats. Write 6 × 2 = 12. That side has 12 seats.

Some problems use *scaling*: one thing is so many *times as many* as another. "Ana's ribbon is 4 feet long. Ben's ribbon is 3 times as long." Ben's ribbon is 3 × 4 = 12 feet. Scaling does not mean groups of ribbons. It means stretching one length to 3 times its size. Draw a bar for Ana and a bar 3 times longer for Ben.

Always check your answer against the story. "Each of 7 students brings 3 pencils. How many pencils?" If you get 10, ask: could 7 students with 3 pencils each have only 10? No. 7 × 3 = 21 pencils. Words like each, per, every and times as many are clues to multiply. Not every problem multiplies, so picture the story first.

words.d: a math question told as a short story
making something a number of times as big; 3 times as long as 4 feet is 12 feet
a phrase that tells you to multiply: 3 times as many as 5 is 15

look.title: Find the Groups
look.text: Read: "A muffin tin has 3 rows of 4 cups. The bakery fills 5 tins." There are two multiplications here. First, one tin holds 3 × 4 = 12 muffins. Then 5 tins hold 5 × 12 = 60 muffins. Now read: "A box holds 2 rows of 5 juice packs. A class needs 4 boxes."
look.prompt: How many juice packs are in one box? In 4 boxes? Show both multiplications.

check.q: Each of 8 tables has 4 chairs. How many chairs are there?
check.why: 8 groups of 4: 8 × 4 = 32. Adding 8 + 4 = 12 is the mistake.

check.q: Rosa's rope is 5 meters long. Tom's rope is 4 times as long. How long is Tom's rope?
check.why: 4 times as long means 4 × 5 = 20 meters. Adding 4 + 5 = 9 is the mistake.

check.q: Which phrase in a problem is a clue to multiply?
check.why: Each signals equal groups, like 4 chairs at each table. The other phrases point to subtraction.

review.q: There are 6 bags with 9 marbles in each bag. How many marbles are there?
review.why: 6 × 9 = 54. Check with nines: 5 + 4 = 9. Adding 6 + 9 = 15 is the mistake.
Four 7s are added, so it is 4 × 7 = 28.

review.q: A theater has 9 rows with 8 seats in each row. How many seats are there?
review.why: 9 × 8 = 72. Check: 8 × 9 by doubling 9 three times is 18, 36, 72.

review.q: Which pair of facts shows the commutative property of multiplication?
review.why: 5 × 8 and 8 × 5 switch the order of the factors and give the same product, 40.

review.q: A rectangle is 6 units by 8 units. What is its area?
review.why: Area is 6 × 8 = 48 square units. Adding 6 + 8 = 14 is not area.

review.q: Which number is NOT a multiple of 4?
review.why: The multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36, 40. The number 18 is not on the list; 4 × 4 = 16 and 4 × 5 = 20.

chapters.title: Division and Fact Families
chapters.bigQuestion: When you split a total into equal parts, how do you know how many each part gets, and what happens to the leftovers?

story.title: Twenty-Eight Cookies, Four Friends
story.kicker: A plate of cookies, a fair share for everyone, and two cookies that would not fit.
paragraphs: Priya, Marcus, Elena and Sam finished their science project early. Priya's grandmother set a plate on the table: 28 oatmeal cookies, still warm. "Share them fairly," she said, and went back to the kitchen. Fair meant the same number for everyone. Nobody wanted to be the one who got fewer.

Sam started dealing them out like cards. One for Priya, one for Marcus, one for Elena, one for Sam. Then around again. Each round used 4 cookies. After 7 rounds the plate was empty, and each friend had a stack of 7. Marcus checked by counting his stack twice. Elena checked a different way: 4 stacks of 7 is 4 × 7, and 4 × 7 = 28. It matched.

"So 28 split 4 ways is 7," Priya said. "That's division. Twenty-eight divided by four." She wrote it on a napkin: 28 ÷ 4 = 7. Sam noticed something. "It's the same fact as 4 × 7 = 28, just turned around. If you know one, you know the other." Elena wrote the whole set: 4 × 7 = 28, 7 × 4 = 28, 28 ÷ 4 = 7, 28 ÷ 7 = 4.

Then Grandmother came back with two more cookies. "I found these in the oven." Now there were 30 to share among 4 friends. Sam dealt out the two extras: one for Priya, one for Marcus. Then he stopped. Elena and Sam had none. That was not fair. They put the two cookies back on the plate.

"Two left over," Marcus said. "Thirty divided by four is seven, with two left over." Priya wrote 30 ÷ 4 = 7 R 2 on the napkin. The R stood for remainder. Elena had an idea. "We could cut each extra cookie in half. Then everyone gets half a cookie more." Sam had a different idea. "Or we give them to Grandmother." That, everyone agreed, was the fairest answer of all.
story.think: The friends found three ways to handle the 2 extra cookies. Which one would you choose, and when would each way be the right choice?

lessons.title: Sharing Fairly
lessons.mainIdea: Division as sharing splits a total into a set number of equal groups and asks how many each group gets.
reading: Four friends bake 28 cookies and want to *share* them fairly. Fair means each friend gets the same number. Deal them out like cards: one for you, one for you, one for you, one for me. Keep going until the cookies are gone. Each friend ends up with 7. That is *division* as sharing, and we write 28 ÷ 4 = 7.

The sign ÷ means *divide*. Read 28 ÷ 4 as 28 divided by 4. The 28 is the total. The 4 is how many groups. The 7 is how many in each group. Dealing out works, but it is slow. A faster way: ask what number times 4 makes 28. Since 4 × 7 = 28, the answer is 7.

Try 30 ÷ 5. Thirty stickers are shared by 5 students. Ask: 5 times what makes 30? 5 × 6 = 30, so each student gets 6. A common mistake is to subtract: 30 − 5 = 25. Twenty-five stickers each would need 125 stickers in all. Check by multiplying back: 5 × 6 = 30, the total you started with.

words.d: splitting a total into equal groups; the sign is ÷
to split a number into equal groups; 28 ÷ 4 means 28 divided by 4
to give the same amount to each person or group

look.title: Deal Out 24 Cards
look.text: Three players share a deck of 24 cards. Deal one at a time: player 1, player 2, player 3, then around again. After one round, 3 cards are gone. After 8 rounds, all 24 are dealt. Each player holds 8 cards, so 24 ÷ 3 = 8. Now try dealing the 24 cards to 4 players.
look.prompt: How many rounds does it take, and how many cards does each player get?

check.q: 18 pencils are shared equally by 6 students. How many pencils does each student get?
check.why: 6 × 3 = 18, so 18 ÷ 6 = 3. Subtracting 18 − 6 = 12 is the mistake.

check.q: In 35 ÷ 5 = 7, what does the 5 tell you?
check.why: 35 is the total, 5 is the number of groups, and 7 is how many in each group.

check.q: Which multiplication helps you solve 32 ÷ 4?
check.why: Ask 4 times what makes 32. Since 4 × 8 = 32, the answer to 32 ÷ 4 is 8.

lessons.title: Making Groups
lessons.mainIdea: Division as grouping asks how many groups of a given size fit in the total.
reading: Now the cookies go into bags, 4 to a bag. How many bags can you fill from 28 cookies? This is division too, but the question changed. You know the size of each group, 4. You want the number of groups. Take away 4 at a time: 28, 24, 20, 16, 12, 8, 4, 0. That fills 7 bags. Again, 28 ÷ 4 = 7.

This is division as *grouping*. Sharing asks how many are in each group. Grouping asks how many groups there are. Both use the same fact, 4 × 7 = 28. The story decides which question you are answering. Twenty cups, 5 to a tray: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 trays. Twenty cups spread over 5 trays: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 cups on each tray.

Grouping is *repeated subtraction*, just as multiplying is repeated addition. To find 24 ÷ 6, subtract 6 until you reach 0: 24, 18, 12, 6, 0. You subtracted 4 times, so 24 ÷ 6 = 4. Count the subtractions, not the numbers you wrote. A student who counts the list 24, 18, 12, 6, 0 and says 5 has counted the starting number.

words.d: dividing to find how many groups of a set size fit in a total
taking away the same number again and again until you reach 0

look.title: Ticket Booklets
look.text: A booklet holds 6 ride tickets, and the fair sells tickets only in booklets. Jada has 42 tickets. How many booklets did she buy? Think: 6 × ? = 42. Since 6 × 7 = 42, she bought 7 booklets. Now think about Marcus, who has 54 tickets in booklets of 6.
look.prompt: How many booklets does Marcus have? Write the division sentence.

check.q: You have 40 apples and put 8 in each basket. How many baskets do you fill?
check.why: 8 × 5 = 40, so 40 ÷ 8 = 5 baskets. Subtracting 40 − 8 = 32 is the mistake.

check.q: Which question is a grouping question?
choices: 21 balloons, 3 in each bunch. How many bunches?
21 balloons shared by 3 kids. How many does each get?
21 balloons, and 3 pop. How many are left?
check.why: Grouping knows the size of each group (3) and asks how many groups. 21 ÷ 3 = 7 bunches.

check.q: Use repeated subtraction for 36 ÷ 9. How many times do you subtract 9 to reach 0?
check.why: 36, 27, 18, 9, 0 is four subtractions, so 36 ÷ 9 = 4. Counting the 36 too gives 5, a common mistake.

lessons.title: The Words of Division
lessons.mainIdea: In 28 ÷ 4 = 7, the dividend is 28, the divisor is 4 and the quotient is 7.
reading: Division has its own names. In 28 ÷ 4 = 7, the number being divided, 28, is the *dividend*. The number you divide by, 4, is the *divisor*. The answer, 7, is the *quotient*. Think of the dividend as the whole pile, the divisor as the way you split it, and the quotient as what you get.

Order matters in division. 28 ÷ 4 = 7, but 4 ÷ 28 is a tiny piece, not 7. Always write the total first. Some problems say divide 28 by 4, and some say 4 goes into 28. Both mean 28 ÷ 4. Division is also written with a bar, like 28/4, which is the same shape you will see in fractions.

Two special divisors are 1 and the number itself. Any number divided by 1 is itself: 9 ÷ 1 = 9, since one group holds everything. Any number divided by itself is 1: 9 ÷ 9 = 1, one in each of nine groups. Zero divided by any number is 0: 0 ÷ 6 = 0, since there is nothing to share. Dividing by 0 has no answer, so we never write it.

words.d: the number being divided; in 28 ÷ 4 = 7, the dividend is 28
the number you divide by; in 28 ÷ 4 = 7, the divisor is 4
the answer to a division; in 28 ÷ 4 = 7, the quotient is 7

look.title: Name the Parts
look.cite: The parts of one division sentence, and three special cases
look.prompt: Why does 12 ÷ 12 give 1 while 12 ÷ 1 gives 12? Explain with a sharing story.

check.q: In 63 ÷ 7 = 9, which number is the divisor?
check.why: The divisor is the number you divide by, 7. 63 is the dividend and 9 is the quotient.

check.q: What is 8 ÷ 1?
check.why: One group holds all 8, so 8 ÷ 1 = 8.

check.q: Which sentence means the same as divide 54 by 6?
check.why: The total, 54, comes first: 54 ÷ 6 = 9.

lessons.title: The Missing Factor
lessons.mainIdea: Every division is a missing-factor problem: 28 ÷ 4 asks what number times 4 makes 28.
reading: Look at ? × 4 = 28. The box asks for a *missing factor*: what number times 4 makes 28? You can count by 4s until you hit 28: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28. That is 7 fours. Or you can recall 7 × 4 = 28. Either way, the missing factor is 7. And 28 ÷ 4 = 7 says the very same thing.

Division and multiplication are *inverse operations*. One undoes the other. Multiplying 7 by 4 gives 28. Dividing 28 by 4 brings you back to 7. So every division fact is hiding inside a multiplication fact you already know. To find 45 ÷ 9, think 9 × ? = 45. Since 9 × 5 = 45, the answer is 5.

The missing factor can be in either spot. 6 × ? = 48 and ? × 6 = 48 have the same answer, 8, because of the commutative property. A common mistake is to solve 6 × ? = 48 by adding: 6 + 42 = 48, so ? = 42. Check by multiplying: 6 × 42 is far more than 48. The answer 6 × 8 = 48 is right.

words.d: the unknown number in a multiplication like ? × 4 = 28
two operations that undo each other, like multiplying by 4 and dividing by 4

look.title: Fill the Box
look.text: The box in 8 × ? = 56 wants the number of eights in 56. Count by 8s: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56. That is seven eights. So ? = 7, and 56 ÷ 8 = 7 says the same thing. Now try ? × 3 = 27.
look.prompt: Count by 3s, find the missing factor, and write the matching division sentence.

check.q: What number goes in the box? ? × 5 = 40
check.why: 5 × 8 = 40, so the missing factor is 8. Subtracting 40 − 5 = 35 is the mistake.

check.q: Which division matches 9 × ? = 72?
check.why: Finding the missing factor is dividing the product by the known factor: 72 ÷ 9 = 8.

check.q: For 6 × ? = 54, a student says ? = 48. What mistake did they make?
choices: They subtracted 6 from 54 instead of finding the factor
check.why: 54 − 6 = 48 is subtraction. The factor is 9, because 6 × 9 = 54.

lessons.title: Fact Families
lessons.mainIdea: Three numbers like 4, 7 and 28 make a fact family of two multiplications and two divisions.
reading: The numbers 4, 7 and 28 are related. 4 × 7 = 28. 7 × 4 = 28. 28 ÷ 4 = 7. 28 ÷ 7 = 4. These four *related facts* form a *fact family*. They share the same three numbers. The product, 28, is always the biggest. In the divisions, the biggest number comes first. Learn one fact and you get all four.

Write the family for 6, 8 and 48. Multiplications: 6 × 8 = 48 and 8 × 6 = 48. Divisions: 48 ÷ 6 = 8 and 48 ÷ 8 = 6. Notice that 48 ÷ 6 = 8 and 48 ÷ 8 = 6 are different facts. Both are true. But you cannot switch the numbers in a division; 6 ÷ 48 = 8 is false.

Fact families make division fast. If you see 63 ÷ 7 and freeze, ask which family 63 belongs to. 7 × 9 = 63, so the family is 7, 9 and 63. That means 63 ÷ 7 = 9. When two numbers in a family are the same, like 5, 5 and 25, the family has only two facts: 5 × 5 = 25 and 25 ÷ 5 = 5.

words.d: the two multiplications and two divisions that use the same three numbers
facts that use the same numbers, like 4 × 7 = 28 and 28 ÷ 7 = 4

look.title: A Family With a Missing Member
look.text: A fact family has 3, 8 and one more number. The product is 3 × 8 = 24, so the family is 3, 8 and 24. Its four facts: 3 × 8 = 24, 8 × 3 = 24, 24 ÷ 3 = 8, 24 ÷ 8 = 3. Now a family has 6 and 42 and one more number.
look.prompt: What is the missing number? Write all four facts in the family.

check.q: Which fact belongs to the family of 5, 9 and 45?
check.why: The family is 5 × 9 = 45, 9 × 5 = 45, 45 ÷ 5 = 9 and 45 ÷ 9 = 5. The biggest number comes first in a division.

check.q: What is the missing number in the family with 7 and 56?
check.why: 7 × 8 = 56, so the family is 7, 8 and 56.

check.q: How many different facts are in the family for 4, 4 and 16?
check.why: 4 × 4 = 16 and 16 ÷ 4 = 4. Switching the 4s gives the same facts again, so there are only 2.

lessons.title: Dividing With the Table
lessons.mainIdea: To divide with the multiplication table, find the divisor's row, slide across to the dividend, and read the quotient at the top of that column.
reading: The multiplication table can divide, too. To find 42 ÷ 6, go to the *row* for 6. Slide across until you find 42. Look up to the top of that column. It says 7. So 42 ÷ 6 = 7. You just found the missing factor in 6 × ? = 42 by looking instead of guessing.

Try 72 ÷ 8. The row for 8 reads 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56, 64, 72. The 72 sits in the ninth column, so 72 ÷ 8 = 9. If the dividend is not in the row, the division does not *come out even*. Look for 50 in the row for 8 and you will not find it. Something will be left over, which is the next lesson.

Use the table to build speed, then let it go. Cover the table and try 36 ÷ 4. Think: 4 × ? = 36. Since 4 × 9 = 36, the answer is 9. Try 81 ÷ 9: 9 × 9 = 81, so 9. The goal is knowing the facts by heart. A student who reads 42 ÷ 6 from the row for 7 will get 6, which is a true fact from the same family, but not the one asked.

words.d: a line of numbers going across the multiplication table
a division with nothing left over, like 42 ÷ 6 = 7

look.title: Reading the Row for 6
look.cite: Part of one row of the multiplication table, used to divide
look.prompt: Use the row to find 54 ÷ 6 and 30 ÷ 6. Why can you not find 40 ÷ 6 in this row?

check.q: Using the row for 7, what is 56 ÷ 7?
check.why: The row for 7 reads 7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42, 49, 56. The 56 is in the eighth column, so 56 ÷ 7 = 8.

check.q: What is 81 ÷ 9?
You look for 50 in the row for 8 and cannot find it. What does that tell you?
check.why: The row for 8 jumps from 48 to 56. Since 50 is not a multiple of 8, 50 ÷ 8 leaves something over.

lessons.title: Dividing With Remainders
lessons.mainIdea: When groups do not come out even, the leftover is the remainder, and it is always smaller than the divisor.
reading: Four friends share 30 cookies. Deal them out: 7 each uses 28 cookies. Two cookies are left, and 2 is not enough for another round of 4. So 30 ÷ 4 = 7 with a *remainder* of 2. We write 30 ÷ 4 = 7 *R 2*. The remainder is the part that does not fit into the equal groups.

To divide with a remainder, find the biggest multiple of the divisor that fits. For 23 ÷ 5, count by 5s: 5, 10, 15, 20. The next one, 25, is too big. So 4 fives fit, using 20. Then 23 − 20 = 3. So 23 ÷ 5 = 4 R 3. Check: 4 × 5 = 20, and 20 + 3 = 23.

The remainder must be smaller than the divisor. If it is not, another group still fits. A student who writes 23 ÷ 5 = 3 R 8 has stopped too early, since 8 is bigger than 5. One more five fits, giving 4 R 3. Always check with quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend.

words.d: the amount left over when a division does not come out even
the way a remainder is written: 30 ÷ 4 = 7 R 2 means 7 with 2 left over

look.title: Bus Seats
look.text: A bus has rows of 4 seats. 27 students climb on. Six full rows hold 24 students. Three students sit in the next row: 27 ÷ 4 = 6 R 3. Check: 6 × 4 = 24, and 24 + 3 = 27. Now 34 students board a bus with rows of 5 seats.
look.prompt: How many full rows are there, and how many students sit in the last row?

check.q: What is 26 ÷ 4?
check.why: 6 × 4 = 24, and 26 − 24 = 2. So 26 ÷ 4 = 6 R 2. The choice 5 R 6 stops too early, since 6 is bigger than 4.

check.q: Which check shows that 31 ÷ 7 = 4 R 3 is right?
check.why: Quotient × divisor + remainder should give the dividend: 4 × 7 = 28, and 28 + 3 = 31.

check.q: A student writes 20 ÷ 3 = 5 R 5. What is wrong?
choices: The remainder is not smaller than the divisor
check.why: A remainder of 5 is bigger than the divisor 3, so another 3 fits. The right answer is 6 R 2, since 6 × 3 = 18 and 18 + 2 = 20.

lessons.title: What the Leftover Means
lessons.mainIdea: The story decides what to do with the remainder: round up, drop it, or make it the answer.
reading: A remainder is not always the final answer. Read the story again. Vans hold 6 kids, and 27 kids are going to the museum. How many vans? 27 ÷ 6 = 4 R 3. Four vans carry 24 kids, and 3 kids would be left behind. They need a van too. So the answer is 5 vans. Here you *round up*.

Sometimes the *leftover* is dropped. Bracelets need 6 beads each, and Lin has 27 beads. How many bracelets can she make? 27 ÷ 6 = 4 R 3. She makes 4 bracelets. Three beads are not enough for another one. Here the remainder just sits in the bag. The answer is 4.

Sometimes the remainder itself is the answer. Lin makes her 4 bracelets. How many beads are left over? The answer is 3. And sometimes you share the leftover: 3 cookies for 4 friends means each gets a piece, which is a fraction. Ask what the question wants: the groups, the leftover, or the amount each. Then decide.

words.d: to add one more group so that the leftover is included, like a fifth van for 3 extra kids
what remains after equal groups are made; another word for the remainder

look.title: Three Questions, One Division
look.text: 27 ÷ 6 = 4 R 3 answers three different questions. Vans for 27 kids: 5 vans, rounding up. Bracelets from 27 beads: 4, dropping the extra. Beads left over: 3. Now use 20 ÷ 3 = 6 R 2 for tents that hold 3 campers each and 20 campers.
look.prompt: How many tents are needed? How many campers sleep in the last tent?

check.q: A ride cart holds 4 people. 22 people are in line. How many carts are needed so everyone rides?
check.why: 22 ÷ 4 = 5 R 2. Five carts hold 20, so the 2 extra people need a sixth cart. Round up to 6.

check.q: Each box needs 8 crayons. There are 30 crayons. How many full boxes can you make?
check.why: 30 ÷ 8 = 3 R 6. Three boxes are full, and 6 crayons are not enough for another box.

check.q: Each box needs 8 crayons. There are 30 crayons. How many crayons are left over?
check.why: 3 × 8 = 24, and 30 − 24 = 6 crayons left over.

lessons.title: Two-Step Problems
lessons.mainIdea: Some problems take two steps; solve the first step, then use its answer in the second.
reading: Mia buys 3 packs of 8 pencils and gives 5 to her brother. How many does she keep? No single operation answers this. *Step* 1: find the pencils. 3 × 8 = 24. Step 2: take away the gift. 24 − 5 = 19. Mia keeps 19 pencils. A *two-step problem* needs the answer from step 1 to do step 2.

Read the whole problem before you start. Ask: what do I need to know first? A class of 24 splits into teams of 4, and each team gets 2 balls. How many balls? First find the teams: 24 ÷ 4 = 6. Then the balls: 6 × 2 = 12 balls. If you did 24 × 2 first, you would count balls for every student instead of every team.

Write a short *number sentence* for each step. Label the answer of step 1 so you do not lose it. Then check the final answer against the story. Twelve balls for 6 teams sounds right. A common mistake is to stop after step 1 and answer 6, the number of teams, when the question asked for balls.

words.d: a word problem that needs two operations, one after the other
a math sentence with numbers and signs, like 3 × 8 = 24
one operation in a longer problem

look.title: Field Trip Lunches
look.text: The trip has 5 groups of 6 students. Each student gets 1 sandwich. Sandwiches come in boxes of 10. Step 1: 5 × 6 = 30 students. Step 2: 30 ÷ 10 = 3 boxes. Now try this: 4 groups of 7 students, and juice comes in packs of 4.
look.prompt: How many students are there? How many juice packs are needed? Show both steps.

check.q: Sam has 4 bags of 6 apples. He eats 3. How many apples are left?
check.why: Step 1: 4 × 6 = 24. Step 2: 24 − 3 = 21. Stopping at 24 misses step 2.

check.q: A box of 36 markers is shared by 9 students. Each student then gives 1 marker away. How many does each student keep?
check.why: Step 1: 36 ÷ 9 = 4 each. Step 2: 4 − 1 = 3.

check.q: In a two-step problem, what do you do with the answer to step 1?
choices: Write it as the final answer
check.why: Step 2 needs the result of step 1. In Mia's problem, the 24 pencils from step 1 become 24 − 5 in step 2.

lessons.title: Which Operation Goes First
lessons.mainIdea: In a number sentence with mixed operations, do what is in parentheses first, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract.
reading: Look at 2 + 3 × 4. Two students get different answers. One adds first: 2 + 3 = 5, then 5 × 4 = 20. The other multiplies first: 3 × 4 = 12, then 2 + 12 = 14. Math needs one answer, so there is a rule called the *order of operations*. Multiply and divide before you add and subtract. The right answer is 14.

*Parentheses* ( ) change the order. They say do me first. So (2 + 3) × 4 means add first: 5 × 4 = 20. Without parentheses, 2 + 3 × 4 = 14. Both are correct sentences; they just say different things. Try 20 − 8 ÷ 2. Divide first: 8 ÷ 2 = 4, then 20 − 4 = 16.

Use parentheses to write a two-step problem as one sentence. Mia's pencils: 3 × 8 − 5 = 24 − 5 = 19. The team balls: (24 ÷ 4) × 2 = 6 × 2 = 12. Here the parentheses are not needed, but they show your plan. When a sentence has only multiplying and dividing, work from left to right: 24 ÷ 4 × 2 = 6 × 2 = 12.

words.d: the rule for which operation to do first: parentheses, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract
the marks ( ) that show which part of a number sentence to do first

look.title: Same Numbers, Two Answers
look.text: 5 × 2 + 6: multiply first, so 10 + 6 = 16. 5 × (2 + 6): parentheses first, so 5 × 8 = 40. The numbers did not change, but the parentheses did. Now try 18 ÷ 3 + 3 and 18 ÷ (3 + 3).
look.prompt: What are the two answers? Which operation did you do first in each one?

check.q: What is 4 + 2 × 5?
check.why: Multiply first: 2 × 5 = 10, then 4 + 10 = 14. Adding first gives 6 × 5 = 30, which breaks the rule.

check.q: What is (4 + 2) × 5?
check.why: Parentheses first: 4 + 2 = 6, then 6 × 5 = 30.

check.q: What is 12 − 6 ÷ 2?
check.why: Divide first: 6 ÷ 2 = 3, then 12 − 3 = 9. Subtracting first gives 6 ÷ 2 = 3, which is wrong.

lessons.title: Estimate to Check
lessons.mainIdea: Round the numbers, find a quick estimate, and use it to catch answers that cannot be right.
reading: An *estimate* is a quick, close answer. Before you solve 4 × 19, think: 19 is close to 20, and 4 × 20 = 80. So the answer should be a little under 80. Now solve: 4 × 19 = 76. That is close to 80, so it makes sense. If you had gotten 46, the estimate would tell you to look again.

To estimate, *round* each number to a friendly one, like a ten. For 6 × 28, round 28 to 30: 6 × 30 = 180. The exact answer, 168, is near 180. For division, pick a nearby fact. To check 63 ÷ 7, think 63 is near 70, and 70 ÷ 7 = 10. So 63 ÷ 7 should be a bit less than 10. It is 9.

Estimating also checks whether an answer is sensible. Each of 8 classes has 23 students. Are there about 40 students or about 160? 8 × 20 = 160, so about 160. A student who says 31 added 8 + 23. Use the estimate to catch that kind of slip. An estimate is not the answer; it is the guard that protects your answer.

words.d: a quick answer that is close to the exact answer
to change a number to a nearby friendly number, like 19 to 20

look.title: Estimates and Exact Answers
look.cite: Estimates made by rounding one factor to the nearest ten, next to the exact products
look.prompt: Which estimates are higher than the exact answer, and which are lower? Why?

check.q: Which is the best estimate for 5 × 38?
check.why: Round 38 to 40: 5 × 40 = 200. The exact answer, 190, is close to 200.

check.q: A student says 3 × 29 = 32. Which estimate shows that must be wrong?
check.why: 3 × 30 = 90, so 3 × 29 must be near 90. The student added 3 + 29 instead of multiplying.

check.q: About how much is 54 ÷ 6? Use 60 ÷ 6 = 10 to help.
check.why: 54 is a little less than 60, so 54 ÷ 6 is a little less than 10. It is exactly 9.

review.q: 24 stickers are shared equally by 4 children. How many does each child get?
In 48 ÷ 6 = 8, which number is the quotient?
review.why: The quotient is the answer, 8. The dividend is 48 and the divisor is 6.

review.q: Which fact belongs to the family of 6, 7 and 42?

review.why: 7 × 4 = 28, and 29 − 28 = 1. So 29 ÷ 4 = 7 R 1. A remainder of 5 is too big, and 8 × 4 = 32 is more than 29.

review.q: Tents hold 4 campers each. 30 campers need tents. How many tents are needed?
review.why: 30 ÷ 4 = 7 R 2. Seven tents hold 28, so the 2 extra campers need an eighth tent.

review.q: Lia buys 5 packs of 6 stickers and uses 8 of them. How many stickers are left?

review.why: Multiply first: 5 × 2 = 10, then 3 + 10 = 13. Adding first gives 8 × 2 = 16, which breaks the rule.

review.q: Which is the best estimate for 6 × 41?
review.why: Round 41 to 40: 6 × 40 = 240. The exact answer is 246.
